subject: Anthropology
title: Naming and Power
description: A fast breakdown of Naming and Power for builders.

hook.text: Columbus called them Indians. They called themselves by their own names. Who gets to name whom is about power.

buildup.text: Naming practices reveal power relations. Colonizers renamed lands, peoples, and languages to assert control.

discovery.text: Personal naming varies culturally too. Some cultures keep names secret; others change names at life transitions.

twist.text: Reclaiming names is an act of resistance. When Indigenous peoples restore original place names, they restore identity.

climax.text: Names are never just labels. They carry history, power, and the right to define reality on your own terms.

punchline.text: To name something is to claim it.

quiz.question: Why is naming considered an act of power?
options: Naming defines reality and asserts control over identity

details.summary: Naming practices carry enormous cultural and political weight. Names can encode kinship, honor ancestors, claim identity, or assert power. The ability to name — people, places, languages — is fundamentally an act of social and political authority.
details.whyItMatters: Naming is an exercise of power. Colonial renaming of places and peoples erased indigenous identities. Understanding naming practices reveals the politics embedded in something as seemingly simple as what things are called.
takeaways: Naming practices encode kinship, identity, and social relationships
Colonial renaming served as a tool of political domination
The power to name is fundamental to political authority

faq.question: How is naming an act of power?
faq.answer: Colonizers renamed continents, rivers, and peoples to assert ownership. Forcing people to adopt colonial names erased indigenous identity. Reclaiming original names — Myanmar instead of Burma, Denali instead of Mount McKinley — is an act of political resistance.

faq.question: How do naming practices vary across cultures?
faq.answer: Some cultures name children after ancestors to maintain lineage continuity. Others avoid naming newborns immediately due to spiritual beliefs. Some cultures change names at life transitions. In many societies, knowing and using someone's true name carries significant social power.
